candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Numbers
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 12:1-15. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On 'Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth' (Num 12:3), Ephrem reads the meekness-of-Moses note as the canonical Old-Testament prefigurement of the Beatitude 'blessed are the meek' (Mt 5:5) and of Christ's own 'I am meek and lowly of heart' (Mt 11:29). Moses' meekness is not weakness but the refusal to defend himself against his own sister and brother; the Lord defends him because he will not. Tewahedo monastic spirituality cites Num 12:3 as the canonical Old-Testament anchor for the cardinal monastic virtue of mätayāqǝbǝr (humility) — the desert father is meek in the pattern of Moses.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Numbers
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Numbers, on 12:6-8. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13. PD. Cf. Heb 3:5-6.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Numbers (c. 365 AD)

On 'My servant Moses... is faithful in all mine house' (Num 12:7), Ephrem reads the Lord's defense of Moses as the canonical typological seed of Hebrews 3:5-6: Moses is faithful as a servant in the house, Christ as a son over the house. The household-of-God image is rooted here; the apostolic writer's distinction between servant and son is exegetically inevitable from Num 12:7's vocabulary. Tewahedo christology cites Num 12:7 + Heb 3 as the canonical doubled-witness that Moses prefigures but does not equal the Son who built the house — the typological gap is preserved.
